faculty.bio: LaRisa Anderson-Horne, Ph.D. is an assistant professor in the department of communication at the University of Utah. Her work focuses on the relationships between religion, media, race, and technoculture. She is a transdisciplinary qualitative researcher borrowing from media theories, digital black religion studies, and critical religion frameworks. She was a Roy H. Park Fellow during the completion of her doctorate from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill’s Hussman School of Media where she was awarded the Outstanding Graduate Student Award. Her dissertation explored religious deconstruction as a digital media phenomenon using interviews, textual analysis, digital ethnography, and text mining. She has presented her research nationally and internationally including with the International Communication Association and the Society for the Scientific Study of Religion. She is currently preparing an academic journal manuscript titled "What Blackness Can Teach Us About Religion and Media" and plans to write a book monograph based on her dissertation research. Department research interests: Critical Race, Feminist, and Cultural Studies; Digital Media and Technoculture. Fields of research: Communication and media studies; Religion, society and culture; Communication technology and digital media studies. faculty.name: Mark Bergstrom
faculty.title: Associate Professor, Director of the Taft Nicholson Center for Environmental Humanities
faculty.bio: Mark Bergstrom is an award-winning scholar, teacher and administrator. Professor Bergstrom is an Associate Professor of Communication at the University of Utah. He earned his B.S. at Washington State, M.A. at the University of Montana, and Ph.D. from the University of Oklahoma. Mark has extensive administrative experience at the University of Utah, having served 11 years as Senior Associate Dean as well as Acting and Interim Dean in the College of Humanities. Mark was the founding Director of the Environmental Humanities Masters Degree program, and was actively involved in the University’s acquisition of the Taft-Nicholson Environmental Humanities Education Center. Professor Bergstrom is currently the Director of the Center and is a passionate leader who has a deep understanding of the landscape of the American West and Montana. Department research interests: Health and Science Communication; Research Methods and Ethics; Rhetoric and Communication Theory.

faculty.name: Suhi Choi
faculty.title: Professor
research_areas: Critical Race, Feminist, and Cultural Studies
faculty.bio: Growing up in South Korea, I belonged to the postwar generation of the Korean Peninsula. I did not experience the war firsthand, yet I have lived with its copious memories. Since migrating to the United States, I have been further intrigued by the notion that collective memories influence the ways in which individuals, communities, and nations negotiate both identities and power-relations in an increasingly complex and violent global community. My first book, Embattled Memories: Contested Meanings in Korean War Memorials (2014, University of Nevada Press), introduces how diverse narratives of the Korean War have competed for hegemony across various media, including newspapers, human bodies, archives, memorials, and statues. My second book, Right to Mourn: Trauma, Empathy, and the Korean War Memorials (2019, Oxford University Press) illustrates how suppressed trauma is manifested at the transient interactions among bodies, objects, and rituals at Korean War memorial sites. I am currently working on my third book, Phantoms of Memorial: A Reflexive Critique of the Korean War Veterans Memorial , in which I articulate grief, loss, and trauma experienced by American veterans of the Korean War in the memory process. Since 2024, I have been an affiliated faculty member of the Center for Health Ethics, Arts, & Humanities at the University of Utah, where I contribute to advancing Medical Humanities as a field of critical scholarship, curriculum, and engagement in higher education....

faculty.bio: Kevin Coe is a Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Utah, where he also directs the Edna Anderson-Taylor Communication Institute . Professor Coe's research employs both quantitative and qualitative methods to better understand political communication, news media, and public opinion. He is the coauthor of two books, The Ubiquitous Presidency: Presidential Communication and Digital Democracy in Tumultuous Times (Oxford, 2021, with Joshua Scacco) and The God Strategy: How Religion Became a Political Weapon in America (Oxford, 2010, with David Domke), as well as numerous research articles . He is also the coeditor of Teaching Political Communication (Elgar, 2026, with Diana Zulli). Professor Coe teaches courses on media, strategic communication, political communication, and content analysis. He is from Tacoma, Washington, and is a product of the Tacoma Public Schools. Department research interests: Political Communication and Public Discourse. Fields of research: Communication and media studies; Political science; Screen and digital media; Culture, representation and identity. faculty.name: Kevin M. DeLuca
faculty.title: Professor
faculty.bio: Kevin M. DeLuca is a Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Utah; the department directory tags his interests as Environmental and Science Communication and Global and Social Movements. His research focuses on the ways communication technologies mediate human relations with the natural world, environmental activism, visual rhetoric and image events. Named Environmental Humanities Research Professor for 2013-14, he developed the book manuscript Creating Wilderness: Imaging Environmentalism's Sublime Object, the first book-length study of the political and cultural role of images in the U.S. environmental movement, examining landscape photography, paintings and video to argue that such images constructed a vision of sublime wilderness that has propelled the movement since 1861. As a Tanner Humanities Center Virgil C. Aldrich Faculty Fellow (2018), his project Activism on the Wild Public Screens of China: Environmentalism, Social Media, and Civil Society analyzed four case studies of China's environmental movement (mass protests, international social media campaigns, image events and a viral documentary), suggesting new practices of resistance in a global surveillance society and how social media fosters pockets of makeshift democracy in China's civil society.

faculty.bio: Danielle Endres (she/her) is a Professor of Communication and Director of the Environmental Humanities Program at the University of Utah. Her research areas are Environmental Communication, Indigenous Communication, and Rhetorical Studies. Her research projects focus on the rhetoric of environmental and science controversies including nuclear waste siting decisions, climate change, and energy transitions. Her work is guided by principles of environmental justice and focuses on how underrepresented and marginalized groups, particularly Native peoples and nations, engage in environmental advocacy. Endres is the author of Nuclear Decolonization: Indigenous Resistance to High-Level Nuclear Waste Siting , co-author of Participatory Critical Rhetoric: Theoretical and Methodological Foundations of Studying Rhetoric In Situ , and co-editor of several books, including the Routledge Handbook of Energy Democracy . The National Science Foundation and several fellowships from the University of Utah have funded her research. Endres is currently working on two projects: analysis of energy justice campaigns in Puerto Rico, and a collaborative project with the Northwestern Band of Shoshone Nation to collect historical archives for the nation. Endres’ public advocacy work includes being a member of the State of Utah’s Hazardous Waste and Radiation Control Board and serving as treasurer of the Utah Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons. I taught at the University of Nevada, Reno, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill before coming to Salt Lake City. My research explores the historical relationships between newspapers and communities, especially in the American West. My teaching includes journalism writing and media law. I served for 10 years on the board of 88.3 FM Salt Lake Public Radio. Earlier service activities included chairing the University Publications Council, advising the campus chapter of the Society of Professional Journalists, serving on the board of the Utah Headliners (professional) chapter of SPJ, and judging the Association for Practical and Professional Ethics' Intercollegiate Ethics Bowl. She is a queer critical/feminist health and media studies scholar with applied praxis contributions to teaching, research, and service. She enjoys teaching health communication, gender studies, and media studies courses. She utilizes Chicana feminist & qualitative approaches to explore Latina/o/x/e cultural health experiences and Latina/o/x/e journalism and media representations in reproductive justice, gendered violence, and social media context s . Her teaching philosophy is informed by social justice approaches, and she is passionate about mentoring students through diverse and inclusive research projects. She is the co-author of one monograph and co-editor of six co-edited volumes. Further, her research is published in several books, as well as in the journals Health Communication, Communication Education, Frontiers in Communication, Communication Teacher, Journal of Applied Communication Research, Women's Studies in Communication, Journal of Media and Religion, Communication Research, QED: A Journal in GLBTQ Worldmaking, and Departures in Critical Qualitative Research . faculty.bio: Arcia Tecun (Daniel Hernandez) is a *Wīnak intellectual with K’iche’, Tz’utuhil, Mam, and Kaqchikel roots, who also holds Afro, Arab, Jewish, and European lineages. They were initially taught by their parents and family clan, and continues to learn through familial relation, and with a rich global Indigenous community. Tecun received their doctorate in ethnomusicology, housed in anthropology at Waipapa Taumata Rau (University of Auckland) in Aotearoa (New Zealand). They are currently an assistant professor in Indigenous communication and critical cultural studies at the University of Utah. Tecun has previously held an assistant professor appointment in anthropology at Utah Valley University, a cultural director position at Tracy Aviary and the Nature Center at Pia Okwai, and a Pouako (Permanent Lecturer) title at Waipapa Taumata Rau. Tecun’s experience spans across Te Moana Nui a Kiwa (Oceania; Pacific Ocean) and Turtle Island/Abya Yala (Americas), including Te Ika a Māui, Aotearoa (North Island, New Zealand), Soonkahni and Yutah (Salt Lake and Utah Valley, Utah, U.S.), the Kingdom of Tonga, and Iximulew (Guatemala). Their interests include global Indigeneities, kava, popular culture/music, eco/food justice, place-based pedagogy, metaphysics, religion, community research, critical theory and more. faculty.bio: Avery is Chair of the nationally ranked Department of Communication at the University of Utah and was named as one of two finalists for the Scripps Howard Administrator of the Year in 2026. During his leadership, the Department has expanded enrollment by nearly 100% (2022-2026) to more than 1,200 undergraduates, launched the University of Utah Asia Campus’s first Communication Master’s Program, established the Edna Anderson-Taylor Communication Institute with a $1.5 million gift. Avery also helped lead the coordination and launch of a new $12.5 million broadcast and streaming studio in partnership with Utes Productions and ESPN (2026). Among 261 national Communication programs, the Department of Communication now ranks in the Top 10 in peer-reviewed publishing, federal grant dollar awards, and national/international awards. The Department is the 11th largest in the country in terms of faculty and will serve a record 9,000-plus undergraduate students for 2026. Avery also serves as Head of the Council of Divisions for the Association for Education in Journalism and Mass Communication and previously served as a Co-Coordinator of Research for the University’s Center for Excellence in Ethical, Legal, and Social Implications, which was supported by a collaborative $8.1 million NIH grant. faculty.bio: At the University of Utah, Jakob D. Jensen is the Associate Vice President for Research, a Professor in the Department of Communication, and a member of the Cancer Control & Population Sciences Core in the Huntsman Cancer Institute. He is a recipient of the prestigious NIH New Innovator Award (2015 – 2020) and a Presidential Scholar (2014 – 2017). His research has garnered several major awards including Best Article in Risk Analysis (2017), AEJMC’s Krieghbaum Under-40 Award (2017), NCA’s Golden Anniversary Monograph Award (twice: 2015 & 2016), ICA’s Young Scholar Award (2013), AEJMC’s CommSHER Article of the Year (2012), and NCA’s Distinguished Article in Health Communication (2008). Professor Jensen’s research has been published in journals such as the Journal of Communication , Human Communication Research, Journal of Health Communication, Health Communication, Public Understanding of Science, Social Science & Medicine, Cancer Epidemiology, & Risk Analysis (among others). Professor Jensen is an expert in health communication. His research focuses on the strategic communication of health information to the public, with a special focus on cancer. He routinely works with public health departments to design and evaluate their campaigns, interventions, and programs. Most recently, he has worked with the Utah Department of Health on the design and evaluation of colorectal and breast cancer screening campaigns. faculty.name: Robin E. Jensen
faculty.title: Professor, Associate Dean for Research in the College of Humanities
faculty.bio: Robin E. Jensen is Professor in the Department of Communication, and Associate Dean for Research in the College of Humanities, at the University of Utah. She studies historical and contemporary discourses concerning health, science, sex, and gender. Much of her research focuses on the rhetoric of reproductive health as it plays out in the contexts of public sex education, (in)fertility, HIV/AIDS, and adolescent pregnancy. Her new book, Productive Forces: The Untold Story of How Women Doctors Changed Gynecology during the Twentieth Century , will be published in 2027 with New York University Press in the Health, Society and Inequality series. In that book and in other recent projects, she has been exploring how appeals to chemical rhetoric are central to arguments surrounding significant social issues such as contraception access, sterilization abuse, and gynecological cancer screenings. She is also the author of Infertility: Tracing the History of a Transformative Term (2016; The Penn State University Press) and Dirty Words: The Rhetoric of Public Sex Education, 1870-1924 (2010; University of Illinois Press). Infertility was awarded the Winans-Wichelns Memorial Award for Distinguished Scholarship in Rhetoric and Public Address from the National Communication Association (NCA) and the Outstanding Book Award from the Organization for the Study of Communication, Language and Gender (OSCLG). Dr. Jensen is also the recipient of NCA's Karl R. Wallace Memorial Award and the New...

faculty.name: Kimberly Kaphingst
faculty.title: Distinguished Professor
faculty.bio: I am a Distinguished Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Utah, and Co-Leader for the Cancer Control and Population Sciences Program, Scientific Advisor of the Inherited Cancer Research Shared Resource, and Director of Cancer Communication Research at the Huntsman Cancer Institute. I have been a professor at the University of Utah since 2014. My research interests are in health communication, cancer communication, digital health, genetic literacy, and informed consent. A major focus of my health communication research is in the context of cancer genetic and genomic information, examining patient responses to cancer risk information and individuals’ preferences for return of genetic information. I am interested in developing and testing digital health approaches such as chatbots to provide cancer genetic services and risk information to patients. I am also interested in implementing strategies to improve the process of consent into cancer-related clinical trials for patients with varying levels of health literacy. Department research interests: Health and Science Communication. Fields of research: Health services and systems; Public health; Clinical sciences; Oncology and carcinogenesis; Genetics; Communication and media studies; Epidemiology; Nursing; Policy and administration. faculty.name: Rachel Lim
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.bio: Rachel Esther Lim (Ph.D., University of Texas at Austin) is an Associate Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Utah and teaches in the graduate program at the Utah Asia Campus. Her research examines how persuasive communication shapes attitudes, decision-making, and behavior in rapidly evolving social and technological environments. Drawing from consumer psychology, communication theory, and ethics, her work focuses on persuasion, artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging technologies, social responsibility, and trust in strategic communication. Her research has appeared in leading journals including Computers in Human Behavior, International Journal of Advertising, Journal of Business Research, Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management, Journal of Product & Brand Management, and International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction . Her current research spans several areas of strategic communication, with a focus on how people interpret and respond to new forms of communication, including AI-generated content, virtual influencers, brand and organizational advocacy, and other technology-mediated practices. Across these contexts, she studies how perceptions of authenticity, responsibility, and transparency shape trust, attitudes, and behavioral responses. faculty.bio: Kent A. Ono is a Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of Utah. Professor Ono conducts critical and theoretical research of print, film, and television media, specifically focusing on representations of race, gender, sexuality, class, and nation. He has contributed articles to numerous journals including: Communication Monographs, Critical Studies in Media Communication, Communication and Critical/Cultural Studies, Communication Inquiry, Western Journal of Communication, Philosophy and Rhetoric, Amerasia Journal, and Journal of Asian American Studies.He has authored Contemporary Media Culture and the Remnants of a Colonial Past (Peter Lang, 2009). faculty.name: Helene Shugart
faculty.title: Professor, Associate Dean for the Graduate School
faculty.bio: Helene A. Shugart is a Professor of Communication at the University of Utah and Senior Associate Dean of the Graduate School (since July 2023); the department directory tags her interests as Health and Science Communication, Journalism and Media Studies, and Rhetoric and Communication Theory. Her research synthesizes rhetorical, media, and cultural studies to critically assess cultural discourses, with recent work examining discourses around health, concentrating on obesity. Her book Heavy: The Obesity Crisis in Cultural Context (Oxford University Press, 2016) interrogates why obesity campaigns have failed, placing obesity in cultural, political and economic context and arguing that current anxieties about obesity reflect the contemporary crisis in neoliberalism and its failure to account for authenticity; it chronicles competing discourses of obesity that arose in response to the failed official discourse. She joined the University of Utah as an assistant professor in 2001, served as Director of Graduate Studies for the Department of Communication (2014-2021), and received the Distinguished Mentor Award in 2022.

faculty.bio: Dr. Liahnna Stanley (Ph.D., Arizona State University; pronouns: she/they) is Assistant Professor of Indigeneity, Native Studies, and Communication in the Department of Communication at the University of Utah. Her research and teaching engage Indigenous queer and feminist studies, Black­–Indigenous relational critique, speculative media and futurisms, and rhetorical criticism. She is especially interested in how Indigenous storytelling, creative practice, and media animate forms of kinship, care, and relation amid ongoing social and ecological crisis. Her teaching approaches the classroom as a relational and collaborative space for building rigorous, accountable forms of critique, inquiry, and practice. Across discussion, writing, and analysis, students are invited to examine how knowledge is produced within uneven structures of race, gender, colonialism, and power. Her courses encourage students to unsettle inherited assumptions, think historically about public life, and engage theory as a way of understanding and responding to the conditions that shape collective life and survival. Her work has appeared in journals including Review of Communication , Women's Studies in Communication , Communication Education , Journal of Applied Communication Research , Text and Performance Quarterly , and QED: A Journal in GLBTQ Worldmaking , as well as in various edited collections. faculty.name: David J. Vergobbi
faculty.title: Associate Professor
faculty.bio: David James Vergobbi is an Associate Professor of Communication at the University of Utah, on the faculty since 1992; the department directory tags his interests as Journalism and Media Studies and Research Methods and Ethics. His areas of specialization are mass communication law, freedom of expression, media ethics, and journalism history, and he teaches courses such as Mass Communication Law and Freedom of Expression. He received the 2019 Award for Excellence in Teaching from the American Journalism Historians Association (AJHA), given annually to a college or university teacher who excels at teaching in areas of journalism and mass communication history, and has served AJHA as second vice president (2014), first vice president (2015) and president (2016). He has been interviewed by ABC News on freedom of expression and free speech on college campuses.

faculty.bio: Sara K. Yeo (Ph.D., University of Wisconsin-Madison) is a Professor and Associate Chair in the Department of Communication at the University of Utah. Her research interests include strategic science and risk communication, public opinion of STEM issues, and information seeking and processing. Her work has been published in journals such as Risk Analysis , Energy Policy , Journalism and Mass Communication Quarterly , Mass Communication & Society , the Proceedings of the National Academies of Sciences (PNAS), and Materials Today . Originally from Malaysia, Dr. Yeo is trained as a bench and field scientist and holds a M.S. in Oceanography from the University of Hawai'i at Manoa. Her training in ecology and the life sciences has been invaluable to her research at the intersection of science, media, and politics.
